title: Yatai etiquette — the real rules
body:
Fukuoka City's own tourism board is explicit: go in twos and threes, not eights. A yatai stall seats roughly 8–10 people total, everyone included — a party of 8 can fill or exceed one on its own, and the city's own guidance warns a large group may simply be turned away. Split up, stall-hop independently, and regroup after.

Tell the owner your headcount before you sit — "Two people, OK?" — and wait until your whole subgroup has arrived before joining the line; sending one person to hold a spot isn't done. Order at least one drink and one dish per person once seated, and don't linger once you've finished — if the stall's busy, someone else is waiting for that seat. Pay at the end by asking for the bill, not as you go.

Cash only at roughly 90% of stalls, so each subgroup needs its own. No tipping — it isn't part of Japanese dining anywhere, yatai included. Stalls run evenings only, roughly 18:00/19:00 to midnight, and skip stormy nights or whenever the owner isn't up to it — there's no way to guarantee a specific stall is open on a specific night.

title: Regional specialties, in one place
body:
Tonkotsu ramen — the pork-bone broth style, born in Fukuoka; Ichiran and Ippudo both still run their original shops here. Motsunabe — offal hot pot, traced to Korean immigrant coal-mine workers using cuts that used to be discarded; finish it with champon noodles. Mentaiko — spicy marinated pollock roe, invented in Nakasu in 1949 by Fukuya, who never patented the recipe, which is why it's everywhere now. Hakata udon — Fukuoka's claim as udon's Japanese birthplace, via a 13th-century monk's milling technique brought back from China.

Seasonal add-on: Itoshima's oyster huts run roughly October through April, right at the start of this trip's window — grilled oysters at simple coastal shacks, worth building into the Itoshima day if the season's begun.
